name: Barstow
editorial_article: "Barstow" is a foundational work of American experimental music by composer Harry Partch, conceived between 1941 and 1955. It is a central component of his larger cycle, *The Wayward*, which documents the transient experiences of American hobo culture during the Great Depression. The composition was born out of Partch's own experiences as a wanderer; while hitchhiking in the Mojave Desert in 1941, he discovered a series of desperate, poignant inscriptions left by hitchhikers on a highway railing in the California town of Barstow. \n\nPartch transcribed these raw human expressions—ranging from requests for rides to declarations of heartbreak and existential hunger—and set them to music using his unique system of just intonation and the microtonal instruments he custom-built, such as the surrogate kithara, chromelodeon, diamond marimba, and boo. Structurally, the work alternates between spoken recitations of these graffiti inscriptions and extended melodic passages that draw loosely from American folk traditions. Over the decades, Partch revised the piece several times, expanding its instrumentation to include more performers and instruments, shifting the tone from the stark, solitary desperation of the original 1941 version into a more complex, multi-layered social portrait. By treating the vernacular language of the dispossessed as high art, Partch created a deeply empathetic document of the "forgotten" American experience, showcasing his belief that the most profound music could be found in the unedited expressions of everyday life.
editorial_teaser: A landmark work of American microtonal experimentalism, Harry Partch's "Barstow" translates the desperate graffiti of Depression-era hitchhikers into a haunting, instrumentation-rich musical cycle.
